doc.title: Nancy Wilson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The Coconut Grove show written for her
summary: She recalls the 1,100-seat room, the Luther Henderson and Marty Charnin show, and knowing it would be right.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Let’s talk about the Coconut Grove, because that was an amazing show.
It’s a great room.
Does that mean, in Nancy-Wilson-speak, “intimate”?

To be as large as it was, it was intimate, yes. It seated 1100 people. It was a big room. It was not a small, intimate room at all, but it was intimate. It was the best room I’ve ever worked in in my life, Coconut Grove.
You had a special show, written just for you, which is the first time that was done, I think?
For me, yeah.
What do you remember about the show? Because it turned out to be a very big deal, in the end. So, did you know going into it, that this was going to be . . .
I knew walking down the – through the kitchen. Before I ever hit the floor, I knew it was going to be. You see me walking through that kitchen. There was no doubt in my mind what it was.
Based on the rehearsal that afternoon?
No. Just that it was right. It was right.
A star-studded audience.
Yeah.
It was a very Hollywood moment.
That part you know better than I do.
Arnie Ar[?] Army Archerd was the host of the evening.
That was good.
And there were a lot of celebrities in the audience. Kenny, your husband, was playing, Ronnell Bright on piano, and a band.
Freddy Martin. I’m pretty sure that’s – yeah, Freddy Martin’s orchestra.
I think so. Because this show was written for you, and this is a little different from everything leading up to it, did you prepare in any way differently for that show?
No. I was just happy to have songs like Don’t Talk, Just Sing and Ten Good Years, because that was the complete package.
Meaning?

Not just standing there singing a song, but when I talk about telling a story: it was humorous, it had every quality that I wanted, it was funny, and Bill Bailey was just unbelievable. I should still be singing that, or start singing it again. But that’s only good – that works with a big band. It was wonderfully written by Luther and Marty. I’m gonna throw some corn flakes in my coffee. I remember that.
